new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikoma is a privative tone language (H vs toneless, syllable = TBU) with no word-stress system: nouns may be entirely toneless or carry more than one H, so neither of the defining properties of stress (one obligatory, one culminative prominence per word) holds, and H placement is lexical (bisyllabic stems: toneless / penult-H / final-H), not weight- or edge-driven. Within the same ISO language, Nata is analysed as a stress-like system (exactly one H = most prominent syllable per word, lexically on sigma2 [retracted to a heavy initial syllable], sigma3 or the final syllable) and Isenye has obligatoriness only (H on stem-initial syllable or on all stem syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Aunio 2010 p. 7: in prepausal position 'the penultimate syllable is sometimes prominent', so final-H stems can surface with highest pitch on the penult; all such surface variants are optional free variation. Aunio 2013: final melodic H in verbs is retracted to a long-vowel (heavy) penult; optional Penultimate Shift in the Conditional. Aunio 2015 p. 6: Isenye may be moving toward regular penultimate stress under Swahili influence, but its mono- and trisyllabic nouns do not fit a penult pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on noun stems (domain = stem in Ikoma/Isenye, word in Nata) and melodic tone in inflected verbs; observations of penult prominence are for prepausal/isolation citation forms. No instrumental stress study exists.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ikom1245 'Ikoma-Nata' (ISO ntk) lumps three varieties — Ikoma, Nata and Isenye/Ishenyi — which Aunio 2015 shows have 'fundamentally different lexical tonal systems': the quoted statement (no obligatoriness, no culminativity, lexical H placement) is for Ikoma proper (Aunio's Serengeti District data, also Higgins 2012 and Aunio 2010/2013); Nata is analysed as a stress-like system (one obligatory culminative H per word, position lexical: sigma2 retracted to heavy sigma1 / sigma3 / final; Anghelescu 2013, Aunio et al. 2019) and Isenye has obligatoriness only (stem-initial H or all-H). Glottolog 5.1 gives no separate codes for Nata or Isenye that I could verify; any catalog entry should be labelled 'Ikoma (variety of ikom1245)' and note the Nata/Isenye divergence.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's characterisation of Ikoma-Nata-Isenye as a tone language (Aunio 2015 existing statement); silent on word stress, so it neither confirms nor questions Aunio's obligatoriness/culminativity claim for Nata. Describes the Nata lect, not Ikoma proper, and explicitly says tonal melodies differ across the three lects (cf. Aunio 2010), which supports keeping Nata-based statements separate from Ikoma.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis (syntax/semantics of the Nata augment) states only that Nata is a tone language with a marked high tone; it gives no rule for word stress and no phonology chapter. Its one use of 'stress' (fn. 7, p. 115) is emphatic/pragmatic stress on a predicate to express degree ('very tall'), not lexical word stress. It also notes speaker-to-speaker variation in H-tone placement and, on p. 11, that tonal melodies differ between Nata, Ikoma and Isenye.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. Minor inter-speaker variation in H placement (e=keróóngoori vs e=kéroongoori 'porridge'), not reducible to the Southern/Northern dialect split (p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works opened describe Nata (the central lect of the Ikoma-Nata-Isenye cline, ISO ntk, E/JE45), not Ikoma proper; Gambarage 2019: 10-11 treats Nata, Ikoma and Isenye as closely related dialects sharing one ISO code but differing in Dahl's Law, vowel harmony and tonal melodies (citing Aunio 2010). The existing catalog statement (Aunio 2015) already separates Nata (obligatoriness + culminativity hold) from Ikoma and Isenye (they differ), so the new Nata evidence supports the Nata side of that statement only. The unobtained Anghelescu 2013 paper is likewise on Nata.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Aunio 2015 statement that Nata satisfies obligatoriness and culminativity (one obligatory H per word); adds the verbal side: H placement in verbs is TAM-driven and edge-aligned (macrostem/word), and negative imperatives violate culminativity with two Hs. Treats the prominence purely as tone; makes no stress claim. About Nata, not Ikoma proper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nata is analysed as a tone language: the single prominent high pitch per word is a high tone (H), not stress. In finite verbs H is a grammatical tonal morpheme or is absent depending on TAM, and it aligns to the left or right edge of the macrostem or the word; nouns and most verb forms have exactly one H syllable (citing Anghelescu 2013), with negative imperatives as the exception (two Hs, e.g. mútáɣinsɔmɛra, p. 69). On long vowels a level H appears only in non-penultimate syllables and a falling H only in the penult. No word-stress rule is stated and the word 'stress' does not occur.
new_statements.exceptions: Negative imperative forms carry more than one high tone, contrary to the one-H-per-word generalisation (p. 55, section 2.9, pp. 69-70). Falling vs level H on long vowels is positional (penult vs non-penult), not contrastive (p. 56).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works opened describe Nata (the central lect of the Ikoma-Nata-Isenye cline, ISO ntk, E/JE45), not Ikoma proper; Gambarage 2019: 10-11 treats Nata, Ikoma and Isenye as closely related dialects sharing one ISO code but differing in Dahl's Law, vowel harmony and tonal melodies (citing Aunio 2010). The existing catalog statement (Aunio 2015) already separates Nata (obligatoriness + culminativity hold) from Ikoma and Isenye (they differ), so the new Nata evidence supports the Nata side of that statement only. The unobtained Anghelescu 2013 paper is likewise on Nata.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Anghelescu 2013 (reported as not accessible) is available from the Internet Archive and contains the strongest word-prosody statement in the set. Quotes for the site, all about Nata: p. 89 (abstract) 'In this paper I argue that Nata has an accentual tone system with three tone types which are lexically specified on noun stems.'; p. 91 'The canonical Nata word has one high-toned syllable. Each noun belongs to one of three tone types.' with rules (11a-c): type I = H on the second syllable unless the initial syllable is heavy (then H on the heavy initial), type II = H on the third syllable, type III = H on the last syllable; p. 96 'I will argue for an analysis of Nata as a stress system, i.e.,…

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on type: every source opened (Gambarage 2019, Lam 2016) and the existing Aunio 2015 statement treat Ikoma-Nata-Isenye as a tone language with a single H per word in the canonical case, and none of the newly opened works posits word stress. One mild qualification rather than a contradiction: Lam 2016 (pp. 55, 69-70) shows that Nata negative imperatives carry two high tones, an exception to the 'exactly one high-toned syllable per word' generalisation attributed to Anghelescu 2013 and to the culminativity property Aunio 2015 credits to Nata; Gambarage 2019 (p. 11) adds that individual speakers vary in H placement on some nouns. Neither work discusses Ikoma proper, and Gambarage notes that tonal melodies differ across the three lects, so these Nata findings should not be read onto Ikoma.

sources.note: Whole paper evaluates the three varieties against Hyman's stress criteria: Ikoma nominal tone satisfies neither obligatoriness (toneless nouns exist) nor culminativity (multiply linked H), tones not weight-sensitive nor edge-aligned; Nata (after Anghelescu 2013) is 'a stress system where high tone represents the most prominent syllable', one obligatory H per word, lexically assigned to sigma2 (retracted to a heavy initial syllable), sigma3 or final; Isenye satisfies obligatoriness only (H stem-initial or all-H) and may be drifting toward regular penultimate stress under Swahili.
